video_title: John Armitage: What Makes a Company Worth Investing In? | Podcast | In Good Company
gist: Egerton Capital founder John Armitage lays out his stock-picking framework: moats only matter with good management, capital allocation and culture; pricing power, high incremental margins and margin cushion drive outcomes; he insists on conventional valuation support (P/E, free cash flow, rejecting EV/EBITDA) and is quick to cut on unexplained disappointments. He admits a poor year after missing a huge trade, holds AI exposure (Nvidia, Amphenol, ASML, two hyperscalers) while disliking the concentration, and warns that AI may create herd effects and that permanent capital breeds complacency.

insights.claim: A moat without the right management gets destroyed; Boeing under its previous CEO and Rolls-Royce before its current CEO are examples of moated businesses that deteriorated.
insights.speaker: John Armitage
insights.so_what: Management-change turnarounds at moated franchises (e.g. Rolls-Royce) can be the inflection point; weigh leadership quality alongside moat.
insights.quote: if you have a moat without the right management you get destroyed and look at Boeing under its previous CEO

insights.claim: Culture and capital allocation are as important as moats: Berkshire Hathaway grew from a closed New England textile mill through capital allocation, while Intel lost its way for years because it did not dare to innovate and saw dominant market shares eroded.
insights.speaker: John Armitage
insights.so_what: Screen for reinvestment discipline and willingness to enter new fields; high-share incumbents with risk-averse cultures are erosion candidates.
insights.quote: culture, capital allocation and mates are all very important

insights.claim: Great companies change over time: Coca-Cola remains a great company with no substitute for Coke, yet it has probably underperformed the market over the last 25 years because it has not come up with a new product.
insights.speaker: John Armitage
insights.so_what: Franchise quality alone does not guarantee stock outperformance; demand evidence of new growth drivers.
insights.quote: there isn't a substitute for Coke, but the fact is it's probably underperformed the market in the last 25 years

insights.claim: Pricing power, the ability to raise prices despite competition, is a sign of something truly marvelous because competition is more intense today (lower trade barriers, technology), and pricing above cost inflation structurally drives margin growth.
insights.speaker: John Armitage
insights.so_what: Track realized price versus input cost inflation; sustained positive spread signals structural margin expansion.
insights.quote: if you can price more than your cost inflation, you're going to structurally achieve margin growth

insights.claim: Some industries are now more exposed to competition than others because of the impact of technology, which is a key filter on which businesses to own.
insights.speaker: John Armitage
insights.so_what: Discount franchises whose barriers technology can erode.

insights.claim: Monopolies and market power are good to own if they have been honestly achieved.
insights.speaker: John Armitage
insights.so_what: Market power is attractive, but legitimacy matters for durability against regulatory risk.

insights.claim: The first filter for any idea is whether it is worth the time: many businesses are fairly priced and there is no point spending effort on them; the second is whether he can understand it.
insights.speaker: John Armitage
insights.so_what: Prioritize research on apparent mispricings rather than covering everything.
insights.quote: many businesses are fairly priced

insights.claim: Armitage avoids drug companies because a large pharma CFO told him they cannot assess whether a phase 3 trial will succeed and just treat trials as a series of options; if the CFO cannot know, an outside investor cannot either.
insights.speaker: John Armitage
insights.so_what: Binary clinical outcomes are an edge-less area for fundamental generalists; avoid or size small.
insights.quote: We just think of them as a series of options

insights.claim: The key analytical task is understanding a business's inherent operating leverage, i.e. what will make it massively out- or underperform expectations; without grasping that, the investment is hopeless.
insights.speaker: John Armitage
insights.so_what: Build models around the few swing factors that drive earnings surprises.
insights.quote: what is it that will make it massively out or underperform expectations

insights.claim: Good models isolate the absolute key factors; too much detail means garbage in, garbage out, and minor assumption changes make everything go haywire. He argues too many leading sell-side analysts leave modeling to juniors.
insights.speaker: John Armitage
insights.so_what: Favor parsimonious driver-based models over sprawling ones.
insights.quote: Too much detail, minor changes of assumptions, everything goes haywire

insights.claim: Airbus (a big holding) is modeled as planes times price, but prices are private and contractual, so the analysis focuses on incremental unit margins, when backlog pricing trends hit revenues, large forecastable costs like R&D, and FX.
insights.speaker: John Armitage
insights.so_what: Watch backlog pricing commentary and incremental margins as the drivers of Airbus earnings; Egerton is a large holder.

insights.claim: For reinsurers (where Egerton has had big holdings), contracts are private, so reserve development history is the key evidence of how well losses were estimated, and in insurance good companies tend to get better and bad ones worse.
insights.speaker: John Armitage
insights.so_what: Use reserve development track records to separate quality reinsurers; quality dispersion tends to widen.
insights.quote: good companies tend to do better and bad companies tend to do worse

insights.claim: A big issue for Nvidia, which makes 75% gross margins, is memory cost inflation in its bill of materials; investors must piece together BOM composition, memory contract timing and sensitivity to a further memory price spike.
insights.speaker: John Armitage
insights.so_what: Memory price spikes are a gross-margin risk for Nvidia; monitor memory contract pricing and Nvidia gross margin guidance.
insights.quote: one of the big issues about Nvidia is memory cost inflation and what it does to their bill of materials because Nvidia makes 75% gross margins

insights.claim: Visa, which Egerton owns, makes 67% margins with clear top-line drivers and costs and little mix effect, making it far easier to model than opaque businesses.
insights.speaker: John Armitage
insights.so_what: Transparent high-margin compounders allow higher-confidence forecasting.

insights.claim: Incremental margins matter because a very high incremental margin relative to a lower stated margin turns small sales overshoots or undershoots into big profit beats or misses; in an undiscovered recovery story you want very high incremental margins because the market rarely dares to factor in their benefit.
insights.speaker: John Armitage
insights.so_what: Recovery stories with high incremental margins are where consensus most underestimates earnings upside.
insights.quote: no one really kind of factors in the benefits of what a really good incremental margin can be. People don't really dare to do that

insights.claim: Accrual accounting is a balance sheet output, so balance sheet and P&L moves cannot be separated; he checks inventories, payables, receivables, cash, and artificial cash boosters such as factoring receivables, as well as accounting policies and depreciation rates.
insights.speaker: John Armitage
insights.so_what: Working-capital and receivables-factoring checks can flag earnings quality problems early.

insights.claim: A key test of management is whether they admit mistakes; Ryanair's Michael O'Leary, despite building the world's most profitable airline, talks as if he had made a series of mistakes, combining relentless detail focus with a strong team.
insights.speaker: John Armitage
insights.so_what: Self-critical managements are a positive signal; Armitage rates Ryanair's leadership among the world's best.
insights.quote: do managements admit their mistakes?

insights.claim: When Pat Gelsinger joined Intel he changed accounting so stock-based compensation was added back to earnings, which Armitage cites as a lack of realism about costs.
insights.speaker: John Armitage
insights.so_what: Treat SBC add-backs and flattering accounting changes as management-quality red flags.
insights.quote: So, so stockbased comp is not part of compensation. It's not a cost. Like really, is that realism or not?

insights.claim: Red flags are consistently missing expectations, a persistent positively biased presentation, and an inability to admit something might be wrong.
insights.speaker: John Armitage
insights.so_what: Serial misses and rosy messaging warrant exiting or reducing positions.
insights.quote: Consistently missing expectations

insights.claim: One of his best sales was Altice, a leveraged French cable/telecom roll-up with little top-line growth, heavy cost cuts and acquisitions; he sold after a slight quarterly miss because the model left little room for error, and companies with low top-line growth make him suspicious.
insights.speaker: John Armitage
insights.so_what: Leveraged low-growth cost-cutting stories are fragile; an early small miss can be the signal to exit.
insights.quote: I'm always quite suspicious when companies don't have much topline growth

insights.claim: The benefit of a high margin is resilience: a sales shortfall does not shoot the P&L to pieces, so businesses must have room for something to go wrong.
insights.speaker: John Armitage
insights.so_what: Prefer high-margin businesses as a margin of safety against revenue disappointments.
insights.quote: The benefit of a high margin is that if you have a sales shortfall, your P&L isn't shot to pieces

insights.claim: Getting too close to management risks paralysis by analysis, a bigger risk today because information has proliferated: every executive comment is analysed globally and must be absorbed defensively, which imprints on the mind and is hard to shake.
insights.speaker: John Armitage
insights.so_what: Information overload can impair conviction; deliberately focus on the key drivers.
insights.quote: you're screwed if you haven't realized

insights.claim: Armitage insists on conventional valuation support (P/E, free cash flow multiples, maybe EV/EBIT) and admits this has made him miss many great growth stocks.
insights.speaker: John Armitage
insights.so_what: His portfolio will lag in momentum-led growth rallies but offer downside protection.
insights.quote: it's probably been too important in my career because I've probably missed lots of great growth stocks

insights.claim: EV/EBITDA valuations are meaningless because depreciation and amortization are real costs; neoclouds are valued on EBITDA though depreciation is their biggest cost, and serial acquirers often over-capitalize costs into intangibles whose amortization is then added back.
insights.speaker: John Armitage
insights.so_what: Be skeptical of neocloud and serial-acquirer valuations framed on EBITDA; look at EBIT and free cash flow.
insights.quote: I hate with a passion EV to EBIT DAR valuations. I think they're meaningless

insights.claim: A good company with decent double-digit growth at near 30x next year's earnings is attractive today, whereas GE at about 35x earnings looks a bit rich to him, even though someone he respects thinks it is cheap.
insights.speaker: John Armitage
insights.so_what: Roughly 30x forward P/E is his ceiling for quality double-digit growers; GE screens as expensive by that yardstick.
insights.quote: if you can buy a good company with decent double digit growth near 30 times next year, that's attractive in today's environment

insights.claim: Permanent capital and long lockups are a trap: they remove the tension of making proper investment decisions and encourage holding collapsed stocks on the assumption investors must wait; Buffett-style drift into quality risks overlooking underperformance.
insights.speaker: John Armitage
insights.so_what: Weekly redemption pressure enforces discipline; be wary of managers relying on locked capital to justify losers.
insights.quote: I think the risk with permanent capital and lockups is that they're a trap

insights.claim: Armitage sees markets as odd: equity markets high, US bond yields high, two wars and oil prices up; without AI-driven growth stimulus and strong US earnings the world would be in a different place.
insights.speaker: John Armitage
insights.so_what: Market levels lean heavily on the AI capex cycle and US earnings; a wobble there removes the main support.
insights.quote: if we didn't have the stimulus of AIdriven growth and if we didn't have strong earnings in the US, the world would be in a different place

insights.claim: He dislikes the AI concentration in markets but participates, owning Nvidia, supplier Amphenol, ASML and two hyperscalers; so much of the US economy is keyed off AI that every portfolio has more AI exposure than it thinks.
insights.speaker: John Armitage
insights.so_what: Hidden AI exposure is widespread; audit portfolios for indirect AI factor concentration.
insights.quote: so many things in the US economy are keyed off AI that inevitably we have we and every other portfolio will have more of it than they think

insights.claim: AI gives fundamental investors instant formatted knowledge and conclusions, but risks a single source of truth if everyone asks the same questions, and may produce a herd effect, which would create opportunities to get away from the herd.
insights.speaker: John Armitage
insights.so_what: If LLM use homogenizes views, contrarian positioning away from AI-consensus answers could earn alpha.
insights.quote: If it produces a herd effect, then maybe you'll have an opportunity to get away from the herd

insights.claim: Overreliance on AI will make analysts' brains rot, as people who stop doing mental arithmetic lose the ability; AI should short-circuit tasks but not think for you.
insights.speaker: John Armitage
insights.so_what: Process edge may come from retaining independent analytical skill as AI adoption spreads.
insights.quote: if you use AI too much, your brain is going to rot

insights.claim: Markets are infinitely more efficient than when he started and AI will speed things up; alpha is definitely much harder, achievable mainly through high concentration in single stocks or themes, which few can do.
insights.speaker: John Armitage
insights.so_what: Expect continued alpha compression for diversified active managers.
insights.quote: markets are infinitely more efficient than they were when I was young

insights.claim: Professional fund buyers favor concentrated portfolios because they run many funds, but they underestimate how disastrous concentration is when it goes wrong; Egerton stays thematically diversified with about 40 stocks, top positions of roughly 6-8%, and avoids financial or portfolio leverage since longs and shorts can both go against you at once.
insights.speaker: John Armitage
insights.so_what: Concentration-chasing by allocators can amplify drawdowns; diversified managers may be out of fashion but more durable.
insights.quote: concentration is just marvelous when it goes right but when it goes wrong boy it's a disaster

insights.claim: Armitage avoids relying on channel checks and alternative data such as credit card data, arguing such results are a function of the more powerful underlying business, though the firm now uses data scientists to integrate AI into its process.
insights.speaker: John Armitage
insights.so_what: Fundamental business understanding over high-frequency data signals suits longer-horizon positioning.
insights.quote: I'd rather not invest in something where, oh gosh, the latest credit card data shows the following

insights.claim: Shorting was very hard during the long low-rate period when everything floated up and any company could raise capital in euphoria, but it has been less difficult since rates went up.
insights.speaker: John Armitage
insights.so_what: Higher rates improve the short-selling environment by restricting weak companies' access to capital.

themes.theme: Process, behavior and a bad year

insights.claim: Egerton is having a pretty poor year after missing a huge trade; rather than chasing the crowd, it stuck to validating the numbers behind its holdings, which paid off as Visa rose about 20% from a point when it was unloved while high-flyers dropped.
insights.speaker: John Armitage
insights.so_what: Capitulating into momentum at the point of maximum pain can be costly; re-underwrite numbers instead.
insights.quote: there was a time when you couldn't give away visa and luckily it's up 20% since then

insights.claim: Egerton performs best in trending markets and stocks and badly in violent moves, which are emotional, often presage environmental change and stem from geopolitics or economic shifts; stock pickers anchored on spreadsheets and recent company meetings are slow to see change.
insights.speaker: John Armitage
insights.so_what: In regime shifts, bottom-up investors lag; top-down risk overlays matter during violent markets.
insights.quote: Violent movements tend to be emotional

insights.claim: In 2008, sitting in London, he dismissed reports of 7% annual US house price compounding as low and failed to grasp the linkages into the broader economy, illustrating that stock pickers can miss that a holding is part of a macro jigsaw.
insights.speaker: John Armitage
insights.so_what: Pair stock-level work with awareness of macro linkages, especially in credit cycles.
insights.quote: if you take one of the legs of the stool away, it can fall to the floor

insights.claim: Being in London risks being late when important things happen in America; Egerton would probably have done better this year if it had been there, though proximity can reduce detachment.
insights.speaker: John Armitage
insights.so_what: US-centric market leadership disadvantages European-based managers in fast-moving themes.

insights.claim: He is quick to cut positions when unexplained results disappoint even if the earnings impact looks minor, as with long-term holding Fiserv, which he sold before it went down a lot; disappointments rarely come alone and he prefers confirmation of a thesis.
insights.speaker: John Armitage
insights.so_what: Treat an unexplained first miss as a sell or trim signal; disappointments cluster.
insights.quote: if there's a disappointment I always tend to cut the position back a bit

insights.claim: Positions start small and grow as conviction builds through questioning, modeling and partner interrogation; a large position requires two people to love it, and new ideas must psychologically displace incumbent holdings, which is harder than it should be.
insights.speaker: John Armitage
insights.so_what: Incremental sizing and two-person sign-off guard against single-analyst overconfidence.
insights.quote: two people must love a position for it to be large

insights.claim: Armitage suspects he has grown more conservative partly because the tailwinds of his early career (falling inflation and rates, the fall of the Berlin Wall, decades of peace) have reversed: economies are maxed out, corporates have done a lot to raise earnings, there are two wars and the West is under threat.
insights.speaker: John Armitage
insights.so_what: Margin and macro tailwinds of the past 40 years may not repeat; temper return expectations.
insights.quote: economies of maxed out. Corporates have sort of done a lot to raise their earnings

insights.claim: After the GFC he worried the firm would be too conservative, so it offered clients long-only alongside long-short; over the long run, if markets rise, not paying a performance fee should help clients.
insights.speaker: John Armitage
insights.so_what: Long-only fee structures can beat hedged products in rising markets.
